issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s eviction suit requiring prior permission is not validly instituted if the Commissioner cancels the District Magistrate’s permission before the suit is filed.
material_facts: The District Magistrate initially refused permission to sue, and the Commissioner later granted it on revision.
The court considered the effect of a Commissioner cancelling permission before a landlord institutes an eviction suit.
issues.conclusion: If the Commissioner cancels the District Magistrate’s permission before the suit is instituted, no effective permission remains and the suit is treated as filed without valid permission.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, permission is subject to an order made by the Commissioner under section 3(3); section 3(4) makes the Commissioner’s order final subject to an order of the State Government under section 7(F). The court agreed with Munshi Lal v. Shambhu Nath Ramkishan to this extent and held that Bashi Ram v. Mantri Lal was incorrect insofar as it said a Commissioner’s later cancellation could not make the suit infructuous.

predicates.eviction_suit_requiring_permission: A landlord filed an eviction suit for which permission had to be obtained before filing.
predicates.commissioner_canceled_permission_before_: The Commissioner cancelled the permission before the landlord filed the suit.

issues.definition: When a landlord files an eviction suit requiring permission after the Commissioner has cancelled that permission, the suit is not maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: A landlord’s eviction suit requiring prior permission is not validly instituted if the State Government revokes the permission before the suit is filed.
material_facts: The tenant moved the State Government to revoke the Commissioner’s permission before the landlord filed the eviction suit.
The State Government’s actual revocation order was made only after the suit had been filed and a decree had been passed.
The court stated that a revocation before institution would leave no valid permission to sue.
issues.conclusion: If the State Government revokes the permission before the suit is instituted, there is no valid permission to sue.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(1) and 3(4), read with section 7(F) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, make the Commissioner’s order subject to the State Government’s order. A revocation before institution therefore leaves no effective permission for the suit.

predicates.eviction_suit_requiring_permission: A landlord filed an eviction suit for which permission had to be obtained before filing.
predicates.state_government_revoked_permission_befo: The State Government revoked the permission before the landlord filed the suit.

issues.definition: If the State Government revokes permission before a landlord files an eviction suit requiring permission, the suit lacks valid permission.

issues.legal_issue: A State Government revocation of permission after a validly instituted eviction suit does not make the suit unmaintainable or the resulting decree unenforceable.
material_facts: The Commissioner granted permission to institute the eviction suit after the District Magistrate had refused it.
The landlord filed the suit after the Commissioner granted permission.
The tenant had applied to the State Government for revocation before the suit was filed, but the State Government revoked permission only after the trial court had passed a decree.
The appellate court set aside the decree on the basis of the State Government’s revocation, but the High Court restored it.
issues.conclusion: Once an eviction suit is validly instituted, the State Government’s power to revoke the permission is exhausted; a later revocation does not end the suit’s maintainability or invalidate the decree.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 3(1), 3(4), and 7(F) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947 contain no provision making a suit validly instituted after the required permission cease to be maintainable because of a later State Government order. Section 14 concerns specified decrees passed before the Act commenced and does not invalidate a decree in a suit validly instituted under the Act. A court will not infer that a competent court’s decree has become unenforceable unless legislation does so expressly or by necessary implication. The court upheld Bashi Ram v. Mantri Lal on the effect of a State Government revocation after institution, while rejecting its contrary holding about a Commissioner’s cancellation; it also referred to Shri Bhagwan v. Ram Chand concerning the breadth of the State Government’s power.

predicates.eviction_suit_validly_filed_after_permis: A landlord filed an eviction suit after obtaining the permission required to institute it.
predicates.state_government_revoked_permission_afte: The State Government revoked the permission after the landlord had filed the suit.

issues.definition: If a landlord validly files an eviction suit after obtaining the required permission, a later State Government revocation does not make the suit unmaintainable or its decree unenforceable.
